item.title: Not All Frames Are Equal:Difference-Aware Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit ASR
item.description: arXiv:2610.22395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods such as GPTQ and AWQ compress large language models effectively, but applying them to automatic speech recognition (ASR) at ultra-low bit-widths (2-3 bits) causes severe transcription degradation. Unlike discrete text tokens, speech activations are highly correlated in steady-state and zero-padded regions yet change rapidly at phonetic boundaries; when all frames contribute equally to the Hessian, static frames dominate calibration and obscure informative transitions. We propose DiffAQ, which computes frame-to-frame activation differences to measure the rate of acoustic change and assigns Hessian importance proportionally, concentrating quantization precision on phonetically critical frames. As a training-free modification to GPTQ, DiffAQ consistently reduces WER across various Whisper sizes and standard benchmarks, with the largest gains at 2-bit precision where baseline methods frequently produce degenerate outputs.
item.dc:creator: Woori Jeon, Jungmin So

item.title: Audio System One Model: Typed Probabilistic Perception of Emotion in Speech
item.description: arXiv:2610.22401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech applications ask many questions about the same voice: which emotion a listener perceives, how aroused the speaker sounds, whether they sound frustrated. Classifiers answer fast, over one fixed label set; audio language models (ALMs) take any question in text, but answer by generation, one pass per question, with poorly calibrated probabilities. We present ASOM (Audio System One Model), a System One model for speech: choice, score and yes/no questions written at request time are answered in one pass, without generation, each with a probability distribution. Frozen speech and text encoders feed a 6.2M-parameter reader with no per-class parameters, trained on listener vote distributions. On MSP-Podcast, ASOM matches a classifier on the same features and data, leads the best of 6 zero-shot ALMs by 0.072 and an ALM fine-tuned on the same data by 0.026, and answers 20 questions in 13.1 ms, 17-41 times faster than the ALMs. It also answers reworded, reduced and new label sets, scales and gender, and on 21 unseen corpora in 13 languages it leads the best zero-shot ALM by 0.138 where the words carry no emotion; where they do, the ALMs mostly read.
item.dc:creator: Jaime Bellver-Soler, Iv\'an Mart\'in-Fern\'andez, Anmol Guragain, Luis Fernando D'Haro

item.title: MedSonor: Learning to Use Clinical Audio in Medical LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.22405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical audio conveys medical information that transcripts may not preserve, but using it in medical responses requires interpreting it alongside clinical requests and dialogue context. Existing medical audio supervision largely targets classification or recognition, while general audio-language models lack specialized medical knowledge and direct feedback for open-ended responses. We present MedSonor, a medical dialogue model integrating medical knowledge, spoken dialogue, and clinical audio understanding. We pair authentic medical audio with clinical requests and combine these audio-integrated dialogues with collected medical audio and synthesized spoken dialogues for supervised fine-tuning, followed by two stages of rubric-guided reinforcement learning. We introduce MedVoice-Dial and MedVoice?AID to evaluate responses within supplied multi-turn medical contexts and to requests involving clinical audio, respectively. Across seven medical benchmarks, MedSonor outperforms the evaluated general-purpose open-weight audio-language baselines and ranks highest in aggregate physician preference evaluation, while broadly retaining general speech capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Geyang Yu, Junying Chen, Benyou Wang

item.title: From Individual Songs to Music Corpora: Evaluating Explainable Harmonic Decision-Making on HookTheory
item.description: arXiv:2610.22416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic melody harmonization is often evaluated through individual compositions or data-driven corpus models. This study examines whether an explainable harmonic decision model developed for individual songs can be applied to independently collected human annotations without changing its rules. We evaluate a frozen Explainable Melody Harmonizer (EMH) on selected HookTheory excerpts containing aligned melody and chord annotations. EMH generates chord sequences from melody alone using explicit criteria for melodic compatibility, harmonic function, persistence, cadence, meter-aware segmentation, and Viterbi-like optimization. Human chords are withheld during generation and used only for post-hoc comparison. Nineteen excerpts yielded 439 evaluable harmonic segments. Exact chord agreement reached 20.50%, chord-root agreement 31.66%, and harmonic-function agreement 47.62%, with functions assessed relative to the key inferred by EMH. Decision-level analysis identified 203 segments (46.24%) where the human chord lay outside the model's candidate vocabulary and 146 (33.26%) where it was available but not selected. These findings distinguish representational limitations from differences in chord selection without treating the human reference as the only musically valid solution. The study demonstrates a reproducible, interpretable approach to corpus-based evaluation of harmonic decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Josef Pavl\'i\v{c}ek, Martin Pelik\'an

item.title: D-Composer: Language Modeling for Simultaneous Drum Transcription and Sound Event Decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2610.22535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Drum beats are often conceptualized and produced as arrangements of repeated single-drum sound events or one-shots. Drum Analysis-by-Synthesis (AbS) models combine this structural assumption with reconstruction-based training to perform MIR tasks such as drum transcription, drum source separation, and one-shot extraction, offering a flexible alternative to more traditional task-specific supervision. However, leading AbS approaches struggle to generalize to a broad range of drum timbres (e.g., electronic drum kits), rely on high-quality paired audio-transcription training data, and do not model intra-class timbral variation within a single arrangement (e.g., multiple kick sounds). To overcome these limitations, we propose D-Composer, an autoregressive language modeling framework that decomposes drum recordings into labeled sound events and their onset times. In drum transcription and one-shot extraction tasks, D-Composer performs comparably to or better than a state-of-the-art AbS system and task-specific baselines while generalizing to a broader range of drum timbres. Our results demonstrate that when equipped with abundant synthetic data and compact acoustic token representations, language modeling provides a simple recipe for unifying transcription and sound event decomposition.
item.dc:creator: Patrick O'Reilly, Saumya Pailwan, Annie Chu, Jason Smith, Bryan Pardo

item.title: PAC-KD: Pathology-Aware Compositional Knowledge Distillation for Respiratory Sound Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.22826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Respiratory sound classification distinguishes four categories: Normal, Crackle, Wheeze, and Both (crackle and wheeze). Existing knowledge distillation transfers four-class predictions without explicitly exploiting shared respiratory events, potentially limiting the transfer of event-specific knowledge across individual abnormal classes and the Both class. We propose PAC-KD, a pathology-aware compositional knowledge distillation framework that learns crackle and wheeze presence through two dedicated specialists. Their complementary knowledge is transferred to a unified four-class student, enabling it to effectively capture pathology-specific attributes while preserving class-level discrimination. Furthermore, stable conflict calibration adaptively regulates specialist guidance according to its consistency with classification supervision, mitigating potential supervision conflicts. Experiments on ICBHI and SPRSound achieve Scores of 65.28\% and 89.54\%, respectively, outperforming strong knowledge distillation baselines on both datasets.
item.dc:creator: Li Xiao, Weiping Tu, Youqiang Zheng, Dan Chen

item.title: Too Emotional to Be Fake? Intra-Utterance Emotion Shifts Expose Failure Modes in Speech Deepfake Detectors
item.description: arXiv:2610.22832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expressive speech synthesis can now change emotion within a single utterance, yet its impact on deepfake detection remains unclear. We introduce EmoShift, a benchmark comparing emotion-stable (AA) and emotion-changing (AB) speech to examine these effects while accounting for static emotion identity and acoustic confounds. It comprises 7,240 bona fide utterances from four source datasets and 9,720 synthetic utterances generated using four expressive TTS systems. Across seven detectors, we find that emotion changes can make synthetic speech appear more genuine, increasing spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points on OMG-Emotion at fixed thresholds. Conversely, emotion-changing bona fide speech increases false-alarm rates by up to 24.4 percentage points on IEMOCAP. Further analyses reveal detector-specific sensitivities to emotion trajectories, not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts. These findings underscore the importance of emotion dynamics in deepfake detection.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Chen, Surya Koppisetti

item.title: Clinically Informed Acoustic-Aware Attribute Modeling for Respiratory Sound Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.22854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated respiratory sound classification (RSC) aims to identify normal and adventitious respiratory sounds, such as crackles and wheezes. Most existing methods formulate RSC as a flat four-class classification problem over norma, crackle, wheeze and both. However, unlike conventional classification tasks with semantically independent and mutually exclusive categories, the commonly used four-class RSC labels have a compositional structure and can be represented by two clinically meaningful sound attributes: crackle presence and wheeze presence. Existing flat classifiers do not explicitly exploit this structure, which may increase the learning burden by treating the four labels as independent targets. Meanwhile, crackles and wheezes exhibit distinct temporal characteristics, with sparse transient crackle events and sustained continuous wheeze patterns, making a single temporal aggregation strategy less suitable for modeling different adventitious sound evidence. To address these limitations, we propose an Acoustic-Aware Asymmetric Framework (AAAF) for RSC. AAAF reformulates four-class recognition as two sound-attribute detection tasks and recovers the final category through logical composition during inference. Built upon a pretrained BEATs encoder, AAAF employs branch-specific multi-layer fusion and asymmetric temporal aggregation to capture localized crackle evidence and sustained wheeze patterns. Auxiliary normal--abnormal supervision and a batch-adaptive dynamic loss are further introduced to improve global discrimination and robustness under imbalanced labels. Experiments on ICBHI and SPRSound demonstrate that AAAF improves overall RSC performance and generalizes across datasets, achieving a state-of-the-art four-class Score of 65.30% on ICBHI.
item.dc:creator: Xinhong Li, Li Xiao, Ziyang Chen, Yuhong Yang, Weiping Tu

item.title: DriftTTS: One-stage Single Step Text-to-Speech via Generative Drifting
item.description: arXiv:2610.22960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-speech models built on score matching and flow matching produce natural speech, but only by calling the decoder many times, which makes synthesis slow. Existing ways to cut the number of calls either distill from a multi-step teacher or add a stage on top of a pretrained model, leaving single-step TTS without a pretrained TTS model unexplored. We question whether pretraining a TTS model is necessary, and propose DriftTTS, which adopts generative drifting, an objective that moves iterative sampling from inference into training. Drifting assumes samples of fixed shape, whereas speech has variable length; we address this issue with segment drifting. On LJSpeech, DriftTTS matches the multi-step quality of Matcha-TTS and RapFlow-TTS in a single decoder call, while being faster. To our knowledge, this is the first application of generative drifting to text-to-speech.
item.dc:creator: Jaehyun Ahn, Dohyun Kim, Heeseung Kim

item.title: Rethinking Magnitude Compression in Spectral Losses for DDSP Parameter Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.22962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral losses for differentiable digital signal processing (DDSP) commonly compress magnitudes, for example by using log-magnitude terms. Such compression mimics human perception, but whether it helps the optimization is less clear, and is usually found only by comparing trained models. In this work, we show that whether compression helps depends on the system's informative region: the region of its dynamic range that carries the information pointing toward the target. To indicate where this region lies without having to train, we introduce concordance, which measures how well a loss orders candidate parameter settings by their distance from the target. We then compare uncompressed, compressed, and combined losses by fitting a modal plate reverb and a subtractive synthesizer model to target sounds. A third system, selected for its low-energy informative region, tests the relationship in the opposite direction. In every system, the loss that matches the informative region performs best: the uncompressed one where the region lies at high energies, and the compressed one where it lies low. Surprisingly, the common combination of both log-magnitude and linear-magnitude terms performs best in none of the systems. Code and audio examples are available at https://github.com/superstem000/compression-analysis
item.dc:creator: Byunghoo Park, Jayeon Yi, Minje Kim

item.title: MUB: An Identity-Masked Benchmark for Music Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.22989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating musical perception in multimodal language models requires separating audio evidence from answers recoverable through metadata or external tools. We present the Music Understanding Benchmark (MUB), a locally assembled collection of 500 identity-masked recordings with existing annotations for tempo, key, time signature, and structural intervals. The collection covers all 24 major/minor key combinations, tempos of 47--180 beats per minute, and 4,676 annotated intervals. Original titles, artists, and platform identifiers are excluded from evaluation inputs. Relative to recent music question-answering and temporal-grounding work, MUB emphasizes scalar tempo prediction and full-recording interval outputs, together with a documented metadata-masking protocol. Saved baseline predictions yield 53.6\% tempo accuracy for a simple DSP estimator and 98.4\% time-signature accuracy for a constant 4/4 predictor. We identify important limitations, including an asymmetric legacy key metric, unverified independent annotation agreement, extreme metre imbalance, and unresolved recording-level rights clearance. No contemporary multimodal language model comparison has yet been completed. MUB is therefore an evaluation resource and protocol under validation, rather than a completed demonstration of model capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Kun Liu, Lyra Tao

item.title: Known Music, Unknown Response: Leakage-Audited Dynamic Arousal Forecasting With Scheduled Future Music
item.description: arXiv:2610.23063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic music emotion recognition usually estimates concurrent or lag-aligned labels from audio that has already been observed. We instead forecast the change in consensus arousal when the upcoming music is scheduled but all later affect labels remain hidden. Evaluation holds out complete songs, encodes each eligible 4-s chunk independently, predicts arousal innovation, and compares the correct future with displaced segments from the same song. On PMEmo and a 1,494-song DEAM evaluation pool excluded from engineering development, a complete past/future MuQ representation raises concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) by 0.389--0.507 over recent affect and remains 0.268--0.382 above a calibrated nonlinear state model. A future-only trajectory contains no past or current audio and still exceeds that state model by 0.150--0.249. The earliest legal future chunk, which ends 5.5--11 s before the target, also remains informative. Correct placement exceeds an overlapping 5-s shift by 0.100--0.209 and the acoustic-nearest eligible same-song segment by 0.078--0.105, with positive song-cluster lower bounds. These results show that both scheduled content and its within-song position carry forecast information under the stated observation rules. The study provides a leakage-controlled reference for known-future music forecasting without treating predictive substitutions as causal interventions.
item.dc:creator: Bin Wen, Dai-Qiao Zhang, Tien-Ping Tan

item.title: PromptSep-Speaker: Generative Target Speaker Extraction via Multimodal Prompting and Semantic Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2610.23066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) isolates a desired speaker from a multi-speaker mixture using cues that identify the target. Prior work has explored acoustic and textual cues, such as enrollment audio and different types of speaker descriptors, but typically relies on a single cue family. Yet no single cue is both broadly available and reliably discriminative. Moreover, most TSE systems adopt mask-prediction models, which are prone to audible artifacts and generalize poorly across acoustic conditions. To address these limitations, we propose PromptSep-Speaker, a generative TSE model based on latent diffusion that unifies four interchangeable cues: speaker temporal order, transcript, enrollment audio, and speaker caption. The generative formulation delivers higher separation quality and multi-modal prompting improves applicability across scenarios. To fully exploit each cue, we further introduce a frozen WavLM representation with an auxiliary alignment loss that supervises query-mixture cross-attention without extra labeling. Across four evaluation sets and a listening study, PromptSep-Speaker achieves state-of-the-art performance over TSE and universal source separation baselines, improving separation accuracy and quality across cue modalities.
item.dc:creator: Yutong Wen, Ke Chen, Prem Seetharaman, Haonan Chen, Oriol Nieto, Paris Smaragdis, Justin Salamon, Zeyu Jin

item.title: X-MDD: LLM-Based Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis for Unseen Languages with Canonical References
item.description: arXiv:2610.23079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) provides phone-level feedback to language learners, but extending it to new languages typically requires collecting and annotating learner speech for each target language. This repeated annotation effort is costly and limits the language coverage of pronunciation feedback. We study whether MDD capabilities learned from annotated learner speech can be applied to languages unseen during MDD training when canonical pronunciation references are available. Our multilingual LLM-based model, X-MDD, uses canonical speech and phones as references to predict the phone sequence actually produced by a learner. It incorporates in-context demonstrations for inference-time adaptation and is further optimized with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using detection F1 and phone error rate. We further analyze how canonical inputs affect prediction and find that (1) canonical speech and phones jointly contribute to actual-phone prediction, and (2) conflicting speech evidence reduces the tendency to copy canonical phones. Trained only on Mandarin and English, X-MDD achieves a detection F1 of 38.07 on Arabic Qur'anic recitation, compared with 44.14 for a supervised challenge baseline trained on Arabic. It also achieves F1 scores of 78.68 and 58.78 on Mandarin and English, respectively, demonstrating effective multilingual MDD within a single model.
item.dc:creator: Xintong Wang, Junchuan Zhao, Ye Wang

item.title: Advancing Sentence-Level Dysarthric Audio-Visual Speech Recognition via Test-Time Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2610.23117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dysarthric audio-visual speech recognition (DAVSR) enhances performance by integrating complementary visual cues. However, existing research is largely confined to word-level tasks with limited vocabularies, which severely restricts real-world communication for dysarthric speakers. Furthermore, performance remains heavily dependent on supervised fine-tuning with speaker-specific data; significant variations in age, etiology, and severity cause traditional methods to struggle with unseen speakers. To address these domain shifts and the scarcity of continuous multimodal resources, we first introduce a "source speech search-segmentation" pipeline to construct a structured sentence-level corpus from raw CDSD videos. We then propose the use of unsupervised Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) for sentence-level DAVSR using Sequential-level Generalized Entropy Minimization (SGEM). Our evaluations across the state-of-the-art AV-SUPERB and ViSpeR frameworks demonstrate that TTA consistently alleviates Character Error Rate (CER) degradation for unseen pathological speakers. Paired t-tests verify that these improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.05), highlighting TTA as a promising paradigm for advancing speaker-adaptive assistive speech interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Shiyao Wang, Hui Wang, Jiaming Zhou, Shiwan Zhao, Yong Qin

item.title: Framing Spatial Hearing within the Free Energy Principle: A Hierarchical Model of Perceptual Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.23196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial hearing relies on dynamic internal representations to decode spatial information from ever-changing acoustic conditions. A fundamental example is sound localisation, where listeners infer the direction of an invisible sound. Bayesian inference provides a computational account of such a localisation process; however, modelling efforts are largely limited to static listening scenarios. Instead, the free energy principle (FEP) describes perception, learning, and action as joint minimisation of variational free energy (VFE), providing a principled framework to account for dynamic conditions. Here, we take a first step toward applying the FEP to spatial hearing. We characterise how listeners' beliefs evolve across trials, in which they estimated sound direction and received subsequent visual feedback on each trial. Listeners are described by a hierarchical generative model where visual feedback drives gradient descent on VFE, updating beliefs over three independent quantities: lateral and polar localisation precisions and hemifield disambiguation. The model captures individual learning trajectories and reveals components with different dynamics: lateral precision improves, as does hemifield disambiguation, consistent with increased sensitivity of the auditory pathway in decoding vertical direction. Notably, polar precision also increases, most for listeners with the lowest initial precision, suggesting that the observed vertical improvement is driven by both hemifield disambiguation and polar precision. This work establishes spatial hearing as a tractable domain for FEP and motivates future closed-loop experiments with full action-perception cycles.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Barumerli, Nils Meyer-Kahlen, Lorenzo Picinali

item.title: Interpreting SSL Representations for Spoof Detection: a WavLM Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.23526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-supervised speech models such as WavLM achieve strong spoofing detection performance, yet which layers encode the most spoof-relevant information and what acoustic properties they capture remain opaque. We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM using the ASVspoof 5 database, combining three complementary analyses: (i) per-layer linear probing with attack-level evaluation across speech synthesis, voice conversion, and adversarial attacks; (ii) a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) linking layer representations to spoofing-relevant acoustic features; (iii) an exhaustive grid search over layer subsets showing that use of five layers outperforms full thirteen-layer pooling. CCA analysis reveals that, while most acoustic features peak in alignment with mid-layers and then decay, voice quality measures jitter, shimmer, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio show the opposite trend, with correlation increasing toward later layers. Embedding visualisations reveal that deeper layers capture a continuous acoustic similarity among attacks rather than discrete categories, suggesting these layers encode fundamental synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 International Workshop on Biometrics and Forensics (IWBF)
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Mallat, Michele Panariello, Massimiliano Todisco, Nicholas Evans, Anthony Larcher

item.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Conditioning, Domains and Failure Modes of Qwen3-TTS
item.description: arXiv:2610.23678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Qwen3-TTS reports state-of-the-art zero-shot voice cloning, but its technical report leaves open how the model should be conditioned, how it behaves outside read speech, and how it fails. We characterise its two cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against Chatterbox, XTTS-v2 and F5-TTS on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control (ATC) speech, using eighteen objective measures, an LLM judge, a spoofing countermeasure and a listening test. Neither interface dominates: ICL clones timbre more closely from correctly transcribed references, X-Vector clones timing, and ICL degrades sharply when a short reference transcript is wrong. Domain explains four times more variance than system choice. Qwen3-TTS leads on intelligibility and pitch register but trails on prosody, and the objective measures rank systems differently from listeners. An off-the-shelf countermeasure flags its clones no more often than genuine recordings, and on ATC radio it fails for every system. Code and audio are released.
item.dc:creator: S\'everin Baroudi, Yanis Labrak, Petr Motlicek, Herv\'e Bredin, Ricard Marxer

item.title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.23745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
item.dc:creator: Koki Ryu, Hitomi Yanaka

item.title: Jarvis: Coordination Deserves a Brain of Its Own in Agentic Interactive Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.23804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive models increasingly hand complex reasoning and tool use to a slow brain in the background, leaving a realtime front model free to sustain full-duplex dialogue. Yet the user may refine, cancel or replace a request while its task runs, so a plan or result that made sense a moment ago goes stale. Each new utterance must therefore be read against the work in flight, but the front model follows only the conversation and the back end sees only its own task. Coordination deserves a brain of its own, one that sees both. We introduce Jarvis, a coordination harness where models judge and code enforces. Its typed decision model, JEV, reads each turn against the live tasks and picks among operations built from a versioned task record. Code checks every choice against the current state before applying it, so no decision can act on a task version the user has replaced. Jarvis also rechecks plans before they execute and results before they are spoken, and counts an answer as delivered only once the user has heard it in full. We build two instances of this design. Jarvis-Audio runs unchanged on three full-duplex speech models. Jarvis-Omni adds vision and rechecks the evidence behind an answer before and during playback, since a scene can change while nobody speaks. With the front model and back end held fixed, replacing Qwen Audio Agent with Jarvis raises tau-Voice task success more than sixfold, from 29 to 192 of 278 tasks, and the gains hold on every benchmark and front model. Against published systems, Jarvis-Audio reaches 69% Pass1 on Full-Duplex-Bench v3 with an open 9B front model, versus 60% for GPT-Realtime. These results suggest that how the two brains are coordinated matters as much as how strong they are.
item.dc:creator: Yuxiang Wang, Shengbo Cai, Zhixian Zhao, Yingda Shen, Yuancheng Wang, Xueyao Zhang, Liqiang Zhang, Teddy Sun, Steve Yves, Zhizheng Wu

item.title: Semantic-Critical Regions for Video-to-Audio Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.23021v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In real-world videos, sound events are often associated with localized and fine-grained visual cues, such as object motion, object-part dynamics, contact events, and interactions between objects. Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods employ implicit conditioning based on global visual representations or explicit control derived from temporal and spatial cues. However, subtle sound-producing and sound-indicative interactions remain insufficiently captured, leaving room for more precise visual conditioning of sound-event semantics and temporal dynamics. Motivated by this observation, we refer to regions containing such sound-relevant visual evidence as Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) and introduce SCR-V2A, a V2A generation framework that explicitly localizes and encodes SCRs as fine-grained visual guidance for audio generation. Specifically, we first identify SCRs through sound-related visual localization. We then transform the localized regions into a control representation through adapter-based dual visual encoding, which jointly captures global visual context and fine-grained sound-relevant evidence. The representation is used to condition a downstream audio generation model. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that SCR-V2A achieves strong performance in distribution matching and audio quality while remaining competitive in cross-modal alignment and requiring few trainable parameters. These results highlight the value of prioritizing fine-grained, sound-relevant visual regions for V2A generation.
item.dc:creator: Yun Fang, Wei Guo, Zhuonan Liang, Heng Wang, Weidong Cai

item.title: Flash RNN-T: Memory-Efficient Joint Network and Transducer Loss Computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.23409v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.
item.dc:creator: Mahmoud Ashraf

item.title: ConvexLLM: Scaling Convex-Hull Speech Interfaces to General-Purpose Audio Intelligence
item.description: arXiv:2610.23539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.
item.dc:creator: Ming-Hao Hsu, Shujie Liu, Yuxuan Hu, Yuxiang Wang, Yingda Shen, Jinyu Li, Zhizheng Wu

item.title: TargetSEC: Plug-and-Play In-the-Wild Speech Emotion Conversion via Arousal-Conditioned Latent Style Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2606.07293v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speech Emotion Conversion (SEC) aims to transform the emotion of a source utterance into a target emotion while preserving content and speaker identity. SEC on in-the-wild data is challenging due to the non-parallel nature of training data and complex real-world acoustics. Existing fixed-duration approaches either struggle to shift the emotion effectively (high quality, low conversion) or degrade speech naturalness (low quality, high conversion). We propose TargetSEC, an embedding-driven latent diffusion framework that generates emotion-focused style embeddings conditioned on speaker identity and continuous emotion. Unlike methods that diffuse over spectrograms, TargetSEC operates in a compact latent space. Experiments on the MSP-Podcast dataset show that TargetSEC outperforms current non-duration baselines and matches or exceeds the duration-prediction baseline in conversion MSE and naturalness without explicit temporal modeling. Demo and code available at.
item.dc:creator: Constantin Alexander Auga

item.title: Dual-BEATs: Unlocking Zero-Shot Stereo Audio Perception in Audio Large Language Models via Dithering
item.description: arXiv:2607.08800v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) have remarkable semantic audio understanding, yet they remain "spatially agnostic" due to their reliance on mono-channel audio representations. Currently, spatial audio perception methods mainly focus on complex room simulations and custom-trained, geometry-aware stereo encoders, which limits their accessibility and generalizability. In this paper, we introduce the Dual-BEATs architecture, in which the left and right audio channels are routed independently through two identical semantic encoders as an alternative to specialized spatial modules. To circumvent the architectural bottleneck where internal normalization otherwise erases the inter-channel variance of stereo audio, we inject a static, uncorrelated dithering noise floor prior to encoding. This dithering intervention establishes a macro-variance floor that "smuggles" spatial geometry across the normalization layers. Evaluated on a ternary directional classification task (Left, Center, Right), we demonstrate that dithered models achieve exceptional spatial resolution--reaching up to 97.2% localization accuracy even on subtle 0.5 panning amplitudes--and demonstrates robust, zero-shot generalization to entirely unseen spatial configurations. Our results suggest that with the appropriate acoustic regularization, standard multimodal models are natively capable of generalized stereo audio understanding.
item.dc:creator: Shuo-Chun Lin, Hen-Hsen Huang

item.title: A Situational Speech Synthesizer for Yoruba: System Design, Phonological Rule Architecture, and Orthographic Extensions for Contour
item.description: arXiv:2607.18317v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present TTSYoruba, a rule-based concatenative diphone speech synthesizer for Yoruba, deployed at online as part of the YorubaName.com open dictionary of Yoruba personal names. The system takes tone-marked Yoruba text as input and produces audio output by applying a hand-crafted phonological rule system to a recorded inventory of 651 diphone units spanning five tonal variants of every consonant-vowel combination in the language. We describe the phonological architecture of the system in detail, including our complete tonal file-selection logic, our treatment of the three-way nasal disambiguation problem (oral /n/, nasalized vowel, and syllabic nasal), and the derivation of contextual rising and falling tones from level-tone input. We also present, as an orthographic contribution, the adoption of the caron and circumflex, which are symbols with prior standing in Yoruba phonological transcription, as standard single-vowel contour tone markers, integrated into the TTS normalization pipeline and the WriteYoruba keyboard input tool. The system's performance was evaluated through a listener study (N=50), with detailed results on Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) presented in Section 6. Keywords: Yoruba, text-to-speech, low-resource languages, diphone synthesis, contour tones, African language NLP, rule-based synthesis
item.dc:creator: Kola Tubosun, Adedayo Oluokun, Hafiz Adewuyi, Dadepo Aderemi

item.title: Sparse Weight and Edge Circuit Discovery in Transformer-based Acoustic Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.10645v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transformer-based foundation models are powerful but opaque, motivating Mechanistic Interpretation methods to uncover the black-box by identifying small computation subgraphs responsible for a task. DiscoGP is a joint weight-and-edge circuit discovery framework originally developed for text decoders. We extend DiscoGP to speech encoders and present, to our knowledge, the first circuit discovery study for modern speech foundation models. Across HuBERT and Wav2Vec 2.0 on several speech classification tasks, we find that the discovered circuits are extremely compact, yet often match or even exceed the performance of the full pretrained encoder with the same downstream head. Through ablations, we show that these circuits reflect pretrained computation rather than random structure or task-head artifacts. We also introduce a memory-efficient DiscoGP variant that reduces the GPU memory cost of edge-circuit discovery at runtime from quartic to cubic. Overall, our results broaden Mechanistic Interpretation beyond text decoders and show that circuit-level analysis can reveal both explanatory structure and unexpected functional behavior in speech encoders.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Jiankun Wei, Ewan Dunbar, Gerald Penn, "Sparse Weight and Edge Circuit Discovery in Transformer-based Acoustic Models," in Proc. IEEE Spoken Language Technology Workshop (SLT 2026), Palermo, Italy, 2026

item.title: Training Music Sample Identification Models on Real Sample Pairs
item.description: arXiv:2609.21911v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sample identification (SI) is the task of matching pairs of tracks, where one track is created by musically transforming an element of the other. In the absence of sample annotations at scale, the dominant training paradigm has depended on artificially creating sample pairs. Although a recently released dataset provides annotations of real sample pairs at scale, an effective training recipe is missing. In this work, we present SI Embeddings (SIE), an SI model that achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, including a large-scale test set. We show that the previous state of the art trained on artificial pairs generalizes only partially to real pairs, and that its training data limits its performance. We also show that real pairs do not fully account for SIE's performance: its architecture and training recipe contribute substantially. We provide the first fully supervised training recipe for real-world SI, establishing a strong foundation for future research in the field.
item.dc:creator: R. Oguz Araz, Joan Serr\`a, Xavier Lizarraga-Seijas, Xavier Serra, Yuki Mitsufuji, Dmitry Bogdanov

item.title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
item.description: arXiv:2610.19869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.
item.dc:creator: Aulia Adila, Yixian Tan, Jonathan Heng, Kunat Pipatanakul, Donghang Wu, Anocha Sutaveephamochanon

item.title: TV-AudioRemover: Joint Text-Visual Guided Sound Removal with Multi-Task Hard-Mixture Curriculum
item.description: arXiv:2609.25864v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visual object removal can eliminate a target from video frames, yet its acoustic trace persists in the soundtrack, causing obvious audio-visual inconsistency. Existing video inpainting models operate solely on pixels, while audio editing models, especially for the sound removal task, are typically driven by text and therefore rely on limited single-modal control, which is less effective than multimodal guidance that provides stronger semantic grounding and temporal synchronization cues. In this paper, we present Text-Visual Guided Sound Removal (TV-AudioRemover), a target sound removal framework that leverages the visually edited video together with a natural-language instruction to suppress the sound associated with the removed visual object from the original audio mixture. To acquire high-quality training data, we devise a pipeline to construct a million-scale dataset of single-object audio-visual aligned samples, from which we synthesize mixture-target pairs customized for model training. To effectively leverage visual context and follow instruction intent, we augment the model architecture with task tokens, generalizable instruction modeling, and modality-specific global guidance. We further adopt multi-task training to strengthen task-role comprehension, and employ a hard-mixture curriculum that leverages semantically similar acoustic mixtures during fine-tuning to enhance fine-grained source discrimination. To support evaluation, we present AV-Remove-Bench, a comprehensive audio-visual object removal benchmark, along with dedicated objective metrics and an MLLM-based evaluation protocol. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both subjective and objective metrics. Project page: https://yjx-research.github.io/TV-AudioRemover/.
item.dc:creator: Xinyue Guo, Jianxuan Yang, Daiguo Zhou, Jiagao Hu, Yuxuan Chen, Fei Wang, Jian Luan

item.title: SpeechCritic: Learning a Diagnostic Speech Judge from Limited Human Preferences
item.description: arXiv:2609.34582v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human speech conveys rich perceptual information, such as emotion and speaker identity, yet most automatic speech quality judges reduce it to a single naturalness score. We study diagnostic speech judges: given two candidates, a diagnostic judge decides which is better, along which perceptual dimensions (e.g., timbre, emotion, timing) they differ, and which audible cues support its decision. Learning such judges is challenging: expert annotation is costly, and simply prompting a frontier audio-language model to produce labels is unreliable: our probing reveals substantial errors and unstable instruction following. We introduce SpeechCritic, which learns a diagnostic judge in a reference-conditioned cross-lingual setting from only about 300 human-labeled comparisons. Rather than replacing the frontier model, SpeechCritic calibrates it with these labels: for each dimension, it selects the acoustic measurements that agree with human judgments, maps them to A/Tie/B probabilities, and passes these to the model as non-binding hints alongside the audio. Compared with the same model labeling without hints, this raises dimension-level agreement with humans by 6.3 points and cuts the mismatch with human Tie rates by 10.4 points. We then train a 7B judge on this supervision and find that different training signals shape different judge behaviors: SFT establishes the task, OPD transfers the teacher's dimension-level strengths and weaknesses, and RL helps most on clear-cut comparisons where human raters agree. Notably, human listeners also find that RL makes rationales cite more specific, localized acoustic cues, although it never directly rewards rationale text. Finally, we show that the pipeline is language-pair agnostic by instantiating it on both English-Japanese and English-Spanish. Together, these results demonstrate a path from limited human preferences to a diagnostic speech judge.
item.dc:creator: Mingyue Huo, Shivam Mehta, Bhavin Jawade, Yinghong Lan, Haoqi Li
